newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 11.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by
The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- AVERAGE STAFF STAKE AT CMG WORTH 100,000 STG

2,500 employees of computer services group CMG have seen the value of their holdings hit a peak of almost 100,000 stg, more than four times the average value at the December 1995 floatation. The rising share price has been fuelled by predictions that companies will have to spend heavily on converting their computer systems to cope with dates in the next millennium and with currency transactions under a single European currency.
-- O'REILLY SELECTS NEW HEINZ BOSS

Chairman and chief executive of the HJ Heinz food giant, Tony O'Reilly, is preparing to step down. There have been fears about his health since December 1995. Insiders at Heinz say that he has settled on William Johnson as the group's new president and chief operating officer. Heinz is set to unveil a wide- ranging restructuring plan which Johnson will be charged with overseeing.
-- PSION CONFIDENT OF MEETING US CHALLENGE

Chairman of hand-held computer group Psion, David Potter, has warned that it faces "a year of transition" when its profit growth will be dented by the strength of sterling. However, he brushed off concerns about competition from Microsoft. Keith Woolcock, analyst at Merrill Lynch, described the group's results as "stupendous" but said investors wanted more details of Psion's licensing plans for the new operating system it is hoping to introduce in the autumn.
THE TIMES
-- HEAD OF SFO SEEKS SHORTER FRAUD TRIALS

Rosalind Wright, whose appointment as the next head of the Serious Fraud Office has been confirmed by Sir Nicholas Lyell, QC, the Attorney General, has pledged to reduce the duration of fraud trials and promised greater disclosure about the workings of the organisation. However, she declined to commit herself to defend the role of juries in complex fraud trials. Critics believe that juries could be replaced by a judge and two or three expert assessors.
-- WASSALL INVESTORS TO SHARE 150 MILLION STG

The manufacturing group, Wassall, plans to return 150 million stg to shareholders as part of a deal that it has described as the way forward for conglomerates, which have fallen from stock market favour as leading companies failed to find the huge deals necessary to maintain their growth. Chief executive Chris Miller said the company was there to create value and not to create an ever bigger company. The payment comes from the group's success in turning round General Cable.
-- DTI SAYS 48-HOUR WEEK LIMIT IS EASY

According to a DTI report, most British companies will be able to adopt Europe's maximum 48-hour working week without jeopardising their ability to compete. The findings contradict the Government's view that the EU's Working Time Directive will be too expensive to implement and damage the UK's ability to compete, particularly with companies in America and the Far East. DTI officials suggest that employers will find little difficulty in implementing key provisions.
THE GUARDIAN
-- INFLATION ON TARGET FOR THE MOMENT

Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George has said that subdued price rises at the factory gate and on the high street are fuelling optimism that the Government will meet its inflation goal in the second half of the year. He claimed that underlying inflation would drop to 2.5 percent by the end of the year. He said that the real issue was whether the economy was on track to meet the target in the longer term. His comments come as an indication that he favours a moderate increase in interest rates to prevent inflation rising in 1998.
-- SUMITOMO SCANDAL KNOWN TO SENIOR STAFF, CLAIMS TRADER

Speaking anonymously, the head of a large London metals firm, one of eight City establishments through which rogue trader Yasuo Hamanaka conducted most of his suspect business, claims that more than 50 officials at Sumitomo Corporation were aware of Hamanaka's activities. He said that over a period of seven years he had discussed Sumitomo's dealings in the copper market with officials of "varying seniority".
-- PLANS FOR UNIVERSITY OF BAE

Chief executive of British Aerospace Sir Richard Evans has said the company may set up its own "industrial university" to make up for the shortfall in technological knowledge which is forcing it to recruit from abroad. He said that BAe was concerned that there was an insufficient number of graduates to call on from Britain, even though the company has connections with 250 universities. Sir Richard said the plan was that the new university would be able to award its own degree.
THE INDEPENDENT -- EMI WARNS OF DANGER OF EURO TURMOIL

Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute, has warned that the single European currency could face an "unbearable strain" in its critical "running in" period. His speech will be interpreted by the financial markets as a fresh signal of a possible delay to European Monetary Union. He said members must have properly met the required budget deficit targets in order to avoid such turmoil.
-- CELLNET SHAKEN AS MD JOINS GROWING EXODUS

Managing director of Cellnet, the UK's second-largest mobile phone operator, Howard Ford, has resigned from his post. He has not given an explanation for the resignation, which came as a surprise to Cellnet employees. The move follows growing criticism of the company's performance in recent months. There are also signs that British Telecom, which owns a 60 percent stake in Cellnet, is moving to impose greater control on the network which it owns with Securicor.
-- TORY GRILLS PIA CHIEF OVER PENSIONS MISSELLING BACKLOG

Joe Palmer, chairman for the Personal Investment Authority, the pensions watchdog, has been attacked by Quentin Davies, a senior Tory member of the Commons Treasury select committee, over the failure to speed up the backlog of 558,000 claims for alleged misselling of private pensions. The chief executive of the PIA, Collett Bowe, said the board had confidence in Palmer's chairmanship. Davis said he was "astonished" by the PIA's failure to make more progress.
